theme: 3 terms on positions in a string: the special index type strings use, moving that index a number of steps, and the crash you get when a position does not exist

terms.definition: The position type a string uses instead of an `Int`, because characters can take up different amounts of memory.
terms.example: You can't use 0 here, a string needs a String Index like `startIndex`.
terms.code:
let word = "Swift"
let i = word.startIndex
print(word[i])

terms.definition: Moving an index a number of steps from another index, written in Swift with `index(_:offsetBy:)`.
terms.example: An Index Offset of 3 from `startIndex` gives you the fourth character.

terms.definition: The crash you get when you read a position that does not exist in an array or string.
terms.example: The app hit Index Out of Range because the list was empty.

video.title: String Index, Index Offset & Index Out of Range | Day 79
video.description:
Learn to explain string positions in Swift: String Index, Index Offset & Index Out of Range, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
String Index - The position type a string uses instead of an `Int`, because characters can take up different amounts of memory.
Index Offset - Moving an index a number of steps from another index, written in Swift with `index(_:offsetBy:)`.
Index Out of Range - The crash you get when you read a position that does not exist in an array or string.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

한국어: 문자열 인덱스: 문자마다 차지하는 메모리 크기가 달라서 문자열이 `Int` 대신 쓰는 위치 타입

landscape.hook: Why can't you read a string with a number? Can you explain it in English?

dialogue.title: Why not just a number?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, why can't `at` just use `n` as the index?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Strings don't use `Int` positions. A String Index is its own type.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because characters can have different sizes?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Exactly. So you start at `startIndex` and move with an Index Offset.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. That's why an Index Offset on a string takes longer for a big `n`.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Index Out of Range. Without it, a big `n` crashes the app.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: But a negative `n` still gets past it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Good catch, that's Index Out of Range too. Check that `n` isn't negative.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So a String Index comes from an offset, and both ends get checked.
Strings don't take an Int, they need a String Index.
